[ { "id": "15906997", "displayName": "Build Low-Latency Distributed Architecture for Scalable Model Serving", "contentDomainCategoryName": "taskManagement", "isContainer": false, "containerId": null, "UniversalAccessControlBlock": null, "activityList": null, "contentEnrichmentData": null, "associatedItemsMetadata": null, "itemVersion": null, "isAssociatedItem": false, "accessControlList": [ { "principal": { "type": "everyone", "value": "EVERYONE", "identitySource": null, "identitySourceEnum": "azureActiveDirectory", "identityType": 3, "identitySourceProperties": null, "metadata": null, "displayName": null }, "ruleNode": null, "accessType": "grant", "transformedIdentity": null } ], "content": { "parsedData": "This feature introduces the next-generation model-serving architecture for our inference systems, focused on minimizing tail latency while supporting concurrent execution of large model families. The current serving stack performs adequately for moderate workloads but shows throughput degradation once traffic approaches the upper bound of the autoscaling window. Profiling over the past quarter identified several pressure points: excessive model load jitter during scale-out events, suboptimal batching behavior under bursty traffic, and inconsistent GPU memory utilization across heterogeneous nodes. These issues increase P90 and P99 latencies during peak periods, which directly affects downstream product teams that rely on predictable response times for both interactive and asynchronous workloads.\n\nThe redesigned architecture will introduce a dedicated warm-pool mechanism that preinitializes model runtimes before they enter service rotation. This approach aims to remove the load-time penalty that currently impacts the first series of requests during rapid scale-up. Additionally, we will integrate a traffic-shaping proxy that distributes requests according to real-time GPU saturation metrics rather than naive round-robin routing. This should reduce the likelihood of hotspots caused by uneven batch construction or resource fragmentation. As part of this effort, the team will also introduce a unified runtime abstraction for GPU and CPU fallbacks so that inference jobs can route to alternate hardware tiers when primary nodes experience temporary contention.\n\nBeyond the serving runtime, the feature includes a new telemetry layer for export of per-model performance data. The existing monitoring endpoints provide high-level signals but lack the granularity required to analyze batch composition, token throughput, or cache hit behavior. The updated design will emit structured performance events via our internal metrics bus, enabling dashboards that correlate traffic patterns with latency anomalies. This will be critical during the consolidation of our inference clusters scheduled for the next release cycle.\n\nThis feature does not include changes to model quantization, tokenizer pipelines, or training-related components; those are being addressed in parallel by the training optimization group. The scope of this work is limited to runtime execution, scheduling, scaling behavior, and performance instrumentation. Successful implementation should provide a stable foundation for upcoming model releases, particularly the expanded series of mid-tier LLMs planned for the fall launch window. Once integrated, the architecture will serve as the baseline for further experiments with speculative decoding and KV cache offloading.", "type": "html", "annotation": null, "semanticContent": null }, The goal of this epic is to introduce a unified evaluation metrics framework that standardizes how training jobs compute, store, and publish model performance data across all research-to-production workflows. Our current pipeline implementation varies by project, with each team defining custom metric schemas, output formats, and storage layouts. This inconsistency makes it difficult to compare results across experiments, automate regression checks, or provide reliable dashboards for downstream consumers such as the Model Review Board and the automated promotion system. The new framework will consolidate metric generation, aggregation, and retrieval into a single set of reusable components integrated directly into the training orchestration layer.

\n\n

The framework will provide a metrics registry, a shared serialization specification, and a set of containerized evaluators that run as post‑training tasks. Centralizing these components removes duplication in individual projects and ensures metric definitions remain versioned, traceable, and reproducible across all model families. The implementation will also support backward compatibility for existing pipelines by providing a migration adapter. This will allow incremental adoption without blocking ongoing model development.

\n\n

Scope for this epic includes the following high‑impact work areas:

\n\n
    \n
  • Create a metrics registry service that exposes model families, metric definitions, and version information via an internal API.
    • \n
  • Develop a standardized output schema that captures training metrics, validation metrics, dataset fingerprints, run context, and training configuration digests.
    • \n
  • Build evaluators that execute in Kubernetes batch jobs and write results to the central store with lineage metadata.
    • \n
  • Integrate the evaluators into our training orchestrator so all training jobs automatically publish metrics to the shared service.
    • \n
  • Provide a migration adapter for pipelines currently writing custom metric outputs, enabling phased rollout.
    • \n
  • Add validation checks that block training jobs from completing if required metrics are missing or malformed.
    • \n
  • Support downstream consumption by exposing recent runs through the experiment tracking API used by the internal dashboard team.
    • \n
  • Document the full specification, including example implementations for vision, tabular, and language models.
    • \n
\n\n

This epic is foundational for improving reproducibility, auditability, and comparability across teams. A unified framework will enable consistent benchmarking, simplify debugging, and ensure that production candidates meet documented evaluation standards.

The goal of this epic is to introduce a unified evaluation metrics framework that standardizes how training jobs compute, store, and publish model performance data across all research-to-production workflows. Our current pipeline implementation varies by project, with each team defining custom metric schemas, output formats, and storage layouts. This inconsistency makes it difficult to compare results across experiments, automate regression checks, or provide reliable dashboards for downstream consumers such as the Model Review Board and the automated promotion system. The new framework will consolidate metric generation, aggregation, and retrieval into a single set of reusable components integrated directly into the training orchestration layer.

\n\n

The framework will provide a metrics registry, a shared serialization specification, and a set of containerized evaluators that run as post‑training tasks. Centralizing these components removes duplication in individual projects and ensures metric definitions remain versioned, traceable, and reproducible across all model families. The implementation will also support backward compatibility for existing pipelines by providing a migration adapter. This will allow incremental adoption without blocking ongoing model development.

\n\n

Scope for this epic includes the following high‑impact work areas:

\n\n
    \n
  • Create a metrics registry service that exposes model families, metric definitions, and version information via an internal API.
    • \n
  • Develop a standardized output schema that captures training metrics, validation metrics, dataset fingerprints, run context, and training configuration digests.
    • \n
  • Build evaluators that execute in Kubernetes batch jobs and write results to the central store with lineage metadata.
    • \n
  • Integrate the evaluators into our training orchestrator so all training jobs automatically publish metrics to the shared service.
    • \n
  • Provide a migration adapter for pipelines currently writing custom metric outputs, enabling phased rollout.
    • \n
  • Add validation checks that block training jobs from completing if required metrics are missing or malformed.
    • \n
  • Support downstream consumption by exposing recent runs through the experiment tracking API used by the internal dashboard team.
    • \n
  • Document the full specification, including example implementations for vision, tabular, and language models.
    • \n
\n\n

This epic is foundational for improving reproducibility, auditability, and comparability across teams. A unified framework will enable consistent benchmarking, simplify debugging, and ensure that production candidates meet documented evaluation standards.

The current automation layer responsible for initiating feature engineering workflows shows intermittent failures when new datasets are registered in the research data catalog. These gaps cause delays in downstream model training jobs and create unnecessary manual intervention by the data science team. Initial logs from last week’s run indicate inconsistent signaling between the ingestion service and the feature computation orchestrator, particularly when dataset metadata arrives out of sequence. This issue affects both scheduled and event-driven executions.

\n

The objective of this work item is to document and correct the underlying coordination problems across the workflow components. The scope includes validating trigger conditions, normalizing state transitions, and reviewing the message handling logic used by the pipeline controller. The resolution should ensure predictable behavior across environments and remove the need for manual restarts during peak ingestion periods.

\n
    \n
  • Trace signal propagation from the ingestion service to the orchestration queue.
    • \n
  • Identify missing or duplicated trigger events and confirm ordering assumptions.
    • \n
  • Refactor handling logic to prevent silent drops when metadata updates are fragmented.
    • \n
  • Validate workflow stability with a sequence of controlled ingestion tests.
